Fred Lipsius

Fred Lipsius has fashioned a diverse career in the music business as a founding member of Blood, Sweat &Tears, a composer and studio musician, and as a member of the Berklee School Music faculty where he teaches saxophone and piano. Fred also produces distinctive computer art and composes poetry based on his personal spirituality.
Fred was interviewed in Boston, Massachusetts on July 25, 2018 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and we are in Boston for the Fillius Jazz Archive and I’m very happy to have Fred Lipsius with me today. And I’ve been looking forward actually to talking to you since 1969.
Really?
Yeah.
Some friend you are.
You never call, you never write.
I never called.

But I think it’s obvious why but when I was a music student I was listening to you play and we’re going to get to that. But I wanted to start out talking about jazz education. You’ve been in the business at Berklee since —
Thirty-three years now.

It’s been my observation in jazz education that many professors of jazz education go now through music school, they might get a master’s, they might get a Ph.D. and then they start teaching. And I felt like you’re a little different because you had some real life experience.
Yeah.
Right?
Absolutely.
Does it make a difference in your teaching?

I can’t judge because I’m not sitting in watching other teachers you know. I’m friendly with a lot of other sax players, there’s about fifteen of them, mostly jazz a couple of classical, in the woodwind department at Berklee. But I feel fortunate, you forget that I © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
came into Berklee at a time when you didn’t need a diploma. Because if you just were good, or whatever their criteria was, you know, so.
You had a resume though. I mean you had things that you could cite —

Well the Blood, Sweat & Tears stuff mostly. I mean arranging “Spinning Wheel” and placing top 10 in the Down Beat and Playboy polls, on alto, which I thought was, not funny, not that I couldn’t play it, but here I am with one of my heroes, Sonny Stitt, a couple of notches below or above him in the top 10 on alto. But it’s a popularity thing and not that I can’t play.

Are we getting a lot of noise from that chair? Good. Okay. I’ll cut that part out. How have you seen the business change, of jazz education in the last ten or so years because of technology. The students that come to you, they’ve grown up in this everything is available on YouTube and on Spotify and so forth. Do you notice a difference in the students?

Well honestly the last ten years or so, I’ve been teaching mostly private saxophone. I’ve taught everything: jazz comp, arranging, all kinds of stuff. But some years ago I had found out more seriously that I had a hearing loss, probably from Blood, Sweat & Tears, from loud amp. So I got kind of panicky and said I don’t know if I can teach anymore. So I started teaching in the woodwind department, fifteen or twenty years ago. So I have my little room with a Yamaha upright piano and two people sit there and that’s it. Most of my students are not — I didn’t ask at the beginning when I was teaching there, but a lot of them are really, that’s not what they want to do is play saxophone. So I do the best I can but I don’t get emotionally tied to them one way or the other if they don’t come in prepared or whatever. You know, I don’t scream at students anyway, I’m just not like that. And if someone does great I say look, you listen to the teacher. I used to go home and tell my wife years ago teaching different classes, I said, “No one listens to the teacher.” I’m just being silly. New York silly. But most of my students are at a lower level. Level eight is the highest at Berklee whether you’re in ensembles or whatever. And I have like beginner improvisers, readers, some kids, they’ve been playing for ten years. I don’t tell them because I don’t want to hurt their feelings but they had a bad teacher in high school or junior high and they were like a band director. They didn’t play, they didn’t know about embouchure, they just gave them a horn, so they learned on their own a lot, and I don’t want to tell them, right, they’re like one year instead of ten years. So I have to start from the beginning. One good thing for me is my sax teacher, I’m kind of going off a little bit — like I say most of the students, they’re not high level, so there’s nothing really to compare yet because they haven’t been out there. I don’t listen very much to, I go on YouTube, I’ve almost stopped because I just want to take a break from that. I still listen to Sonny Stitt, my heroes, Bird and all the old jazz players and some © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

new people. Personally I’m at a point in my life I don’t really want to be putting anybody down. We all have opinions, what we like, just like foods or, why did I pick my wife? You know? That simple. But as some spiritual master said a while back, and I try to live these principles now, you know instead of bringing out the bad in someone, if you have something bad to say, bring out the good, even if they’re bad people. Because it’s going to bring out the better in you and it’s going to maybe open their hearts a little more and you might change that person. So that’s kind of a whole other trip.
Do you have a way to set these students up when you start teaching them improvisation so that it will be likely that they will play something they’re comfortable with?

Down the hall I used to teach a lab for improv, beginning and intermediate levels, two different, maybe eight or ten students, woodwind students, flute, you know, sax, clarinet, even a bassoon once. I had to re-write some music in bass clef. And you know to get someone that can even play a little bebop is crazy [scats] it’s like no one could do that. It’s rare you know. But anyway, but I have about a fifteen page, or thirty page improv workbook that I wrote for Berklee. And like I tell the students the first lesson, “There’s about ten or fifteen good teachers here, like myself, or players like myself, and each person has their own way to present jazz to you. I start with chords and scales you know. That’s basic in music. Some people might just do blues. I’m not teaching just by ear. That’s not my thing. And I’ve had some students in ensembles that have real good ears and play good, so I don’t think I have too much to teach them because they’re naturally talented. Not everybody is with a good ear. But I have this book. So I start with chords. The first page is all the seven or eight different types of chords you see in the fake book or Real Book, standard tunes; major seventh, diminished, whatever. In the key of C and it’s just demonstrated with the tension notes, the ninths, elevenths, thirteenths. Chord tones and tensions. And then on the right side of the page I have the chord scales that they teach at Berklee. I think Phil Woods years ago did a clinic, no he was playing a performance with Hal Crook, one of the great trombone players, teaches here. And I laughed. He was playing acoustically first of all, in a big auditorium that holds a thousand people. And he says, “You know, kids, it’s not all 2-5-1.” And I thought that was very cute and funny. Because jazz tunes have 2-5s in them you know. And he didn’t go into that chord scales. But in those days they had a tee shirt in black and white that had all 2-5 progressions, front and back you know. But I didn’t learn chord scales. It was funny I told some students years ago, I was walking down the street from one building to the next to teach. And a teacher, a piano player, I think it was Mike — I don’t want to get the name wrong, so, I don’t know if he’s still here. He’s a little older than me. But he went to Berklee when I did, in 1961. I only went for a few months. And I remember he had nice voicings and big hands. And I said, I’m just walking down the street to the next class and © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

I said, “Who came up with chord scales?” And he says, “I did.” This was crazy. This was like 300, 500 teachers back when I was talking to him. Now there’s about 800 teachers with the Conservatory merging in the last year or two with Berklee, the Boston Conservatory. But out of all the teachers, “I did.” And my first book for Warner Brothers Music, it’s about a 250 page book on improvisation, The Complete Book of Creative Improvisation. I call, instead of chord scales I say “scales to blow off.” To improvise off. And I said look, to my beginning students or whoever, whatever level, I said, “You don’t have to know chord scales, it’s a thing, I use it because it’s a helpful tool. If you have talent and you can move beyond that” — when I listen to Coltrane and Bird, I’d notate their solos, whatever I could as I was developing my ear when I was 14, 15. And I’d hear oh, it’s a ninth or something you know. Because my original saxophone teacher that taught Stan Getz back in the Bronx, Bill Shiner, he wasn’t an improviser. Beautiful sound on the saxophone. You’d be jealous. Just fill up the room with beautiful, old fashioned, with a little vibrato sound. And that’s this legacy, I have some of that. I have this sound. I think it’s a beautiful sound. I’ve gotten a lot of compliments, and it’s the one thing I feel I can give any student. And I tell my wife, I feel fulfilled if they don’t go any further with jazz or anything, if you’re getting my sound. Because I used to joke with them I said, “I’m not going to buy your CD if you don’t have a nice sound.” Because to me you’re not showing that you’re a good musician. Play classical, jazz, fusion, whatever you want to play, but have a nice sound that appeals to the ear. But Bill Shiner had that. And so I give them a lesson about embouchure. I say it’s just diaphragm and the lower lip. I don’t even care about the upper lip. Although my teacher taught me to play a certain way. I say you have the lower lip, I said I did everything wrong on saxophone with a great teacher. I used to clamp on the reed. And I had this, what someone called a peashooter sound, in a bad way. It was very small. And this is funny, I used to think when I was 14 years old, I’d blame it on my mother. I says, “Are you really my mom?” Because I’m this skinny little, tiny little kid with no sound. So I’m blaming it on my mom.
Did you actually play with your upper lip under your teeth?

Well he had, put your head down a little bit, you know he taught Stan Getz and all his students. But I don’t think you need this other than support and with the slightest support, just be centered in the middle of the mouthpiece. But I have a friend, Noah Brandmark that played with Woody Herman, that had a great sound. And it took me until I was about 30 to have a sound like him, and he was 14 when we met. He was only studying a half year with Bill Shiner and he had this mature sound. I wasn’t jealous we were just close friends. But he’d play over here. We’d be silly. He’d play anywhere and get a great sound. And I could do that now too. If you have the pressure from the reed, you know, what makes the reed vibrate? It’s just this — if you had a piece of wood and air going © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

through it you don’t need your lip. I’m being silly. Or cardboard. And make it vibrate. I was just clamping on the opening of the reed. So I have them start from nothing and blow, and blow as full as you can, but when your lip is on the reed if you’re not putting any pressure at all it’s not going to vibrate yet. So I said slowly get tighter and eventually clamp the reed. And back off slowly until you are vibrating. And you’re getting like, I call it a buzz like in your oral cavity. I can’t explain it. But it’s ahh, like an opera singer, where you’re getting the fullest sound and you’re not doing anything, you have enough air to support it, like a good faucet that works, if you want full volume you can play loud, but you should get that buzz on a soft note too, like [scats] you know? Whatever. And they find the center and all of a sudden for the first time in their life they get the sound and they sound like me for a minute. Like on a G, like a good note, not too low, not too high because C is a little funny. A G — I says, “You got it.” I said I don’t have to say anything more. Now you know.
Memorize what that feels like.

And I’m happy. I said — and then if they’re playing a little soft I say, “Look,” I play my horn, I said, “This is what a professional volume is.” I’m not bragging. And I fill up the room. I play soft too. I say, “Look” I start with a buzz [scats]. And I give them a couple of hints that I thought of, no one told me this. Two things to think about. Because I remember playing clarinet or alto, like it’s a little mouthpiece, when I was 14 or 15, so you’re blowing into this mouthpiece and you’re trying to do something. Think of it as the wall right over here because in the room where I teach the wall is right there. I say imagine you’re playing to the wall. Forget about the mouthpiece. You go [scats] sing it out. Or, imagine you’re on stage at Carnegie Hall or Symphony Hall, and audience or no audience, you’re playing to someone in the balcony. And just sing out the note. Don’t overblow but just sing it out and try to hear it nice and full [scats]. Any note. And they do that. So if they get the note once I say man you’ve got it. It’s up to you. That’s what you have to do. And you don’t have to play loud all the time, but if you’re playing in a sax section lead alto, you need to play full or you’re going to sound like an inner part. So that’s what I give to them. Most of them can’t improvise, that I’ve been teaching. I back them up on piano a lot and we play standard tunes. And in the last couple of years I felt, and I’ve told the students, I think I’ve been teaching wrong, jazz. The wrong approach for a long time. There’s no right or wrong approach. But now I give them some old tunes, like “Jada” or which “Doxy” is based on, I don’t know if you knew that you know. And I point it out to them. I have them play both melodies or whatever. But some of the old standard tunes, the Louis Armstrong in say 1930s, just great, beautiful melodies, and without getting into “Confirmation” and great Charlie Parker tunes, let’s start with something simple. A great melody. And I tell them too, I’m very melodic, and I think this © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

helped me with Blood, Sweat & Tears, everything in my life, who I am. Because I like to bridge to people. It’s not for the pat on the back, “Fred you sound great.” It’s because I care about people. So I always believed that Dick Halligan and myself as arrangers for Blood, Sweat & Tears and the original, not quite a leader, Al Kooper, I think we all care about bridging. And I don’t think every jazz player does care about that. So if you don’t dig it man, you know, whatever. I don’t know. I’m just into, and it’s not for someone to say, “Fred you play great.” I know I can play. It’s just to communicate. That’s the way I am. Maybe I had good parents. I don’t know.
Were your parents supportive of a career in music?
Yeah.
That’s nice.

My dad was funny. He was in the printing business with a couple of his brothers. And once in a while he’d say, when I was listening to Benny Goodman, my first hero, and he’d go like this, “You blow that thing.” And he would forget it was a clarinet or something. But they were good. They got me a silver clarinet when I first started. I made the music class in the fourth grade. And the funny thing was they played for about 40 of us. There was a piano and the teacher said, “Okay kids. Is this the same note?” [scats] “Or a different note?” [scats] And a lot of kids got it wrong. I’m laughing but I got it right. That’s all I remember from the test. So I was in the fifth and sixth grade music class. Mostly violinists. There was about 40 kids. And I played clarinet. And the first year literally I was the worst clarinet player because I was this tiny little kid that loved to play basketball. So when I played my clarinet, I practiced 20 minutes a day. Now it takes 5 minutes to put the horn together with the cork grease and everything, and 5 minutes to put it away. And I want to go out and put on my sneakers and play. So I probably played 15 minutes, 10 or 15 minutes. But at the end of the year the clarinet teacher that came in, he wasn’t the teacher there, he came in a private room in the back. He’d teach about 10 of us. But when you’re in the fifth grade, a little tiny kid, there are these twins and when we played, you’d play a tune like “Lightly Row” so we’d play like this [scats]. You take a breath for every note. It was cute when I think about it now. So they’d make me laugh, looking at other kids, and I was probably the worst. But the teacher would get us in front of our regular teacher, our homeroom teacher, who was a piano player, a very sweet lady, and we’d play for the rest of the class. Twenty violinists and one or two viola players or whatever. And we’d stand up there and challenge each other. We’d play some tune. And the clarinet teacher would pick who was the best. So at the end of the semester he wrote in my yearbook, “Practice more.” It was cute you know. And for some reason, I really don’t remember, I started to practice more, and I became about the second best clarinetist in the class. And I remember hearing people in the project where I lived, in Parkchester in © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

the Bronx, thousands of kids. And there were a couple of kids that played, they were playing sort of Benny Goodman tunes, I mean much better than me. I could barely play anything improvising. I was listening to Benny Goodman, my first hero, and trying to copy a couple of licks. I didn’t have any ear, I could play a couple of licks and I felt great. I mean three or four licks, that was it. But as a little kid you feel wonderful that you can do anything. Or play a tune, “Sing, Sing, Sing” you know. But I remember some kids, I started to pass them as I got the next year or two or three you know. They weren’t so great anymore you know. I remember my brother’s friend was playing “Tenderly” on alto when I first started playing alto, a couple of years later, after the clarinet. And if I could even play the melody, forget about intonation or anything, you know.
They stayed where they were and you got better.
Well they might have still improved but I just — zoom, like “Star Wars.” Getting away from the enemy.
Was there an aha moment or an epiphany or something along the way that caused you do get better like that?

Not get better, but two things that I’m going to mention at this clinic I’m doing for mostly rock & rollers, a couple of jazzers, this Friday, a couple of days from now, in Northampton, that I had mentioned to you. I was asked to do a clinic. So I’m going to talk about “Spinning Wheel” and the importance of an arrangement to make good music. That’s a good question. I’m forgetting your question. Oh an aha moment. First of all, when I was a little kid I remember being in the crib, I’m the middle kid, and my mother used to play radio, and at three years old, if I remember correctly, I’d be touched by music I’d hear like a “Gone With the Wind” theme on the French horn [scats] you know. And I don’t know if I cried, I mean I was just a little kid, but music has always been there. And two guys from Blood, Sweat & Tears, Lew Soloff, who you’ll probably mention later, and Alan Rubin, who sat in with the band and played on “Spinning Wheel” when Chuck Winfield was out. He had a problem with his lip or his son was born or something, so Alan played on “Spinning Wheel.” But those two guys, somewhere during the time I was with Blood, Sweat & Tears, they said, “You’re a natural, Fred.” I don’t know that they knew my background but they said like, “No one made you practice.” I said, “That’s true.” You just had the love for music. Like one of them said my dad or mom made me practice or something. I don’t know that. I felt a little hurt that they were pushed. Because I didn’t have that from my parents you know. My mom used to say, “Are you still in there practicing?” Where I lived in the project I could only play an hour a day because the neighbors complained. And when we moved it was in the lease: your son can only play an hour a day.
Oh it was in the lease. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

Yeah, when we moved to another place. Because someone had complained. They got a complaint, I used to go to school with him, his son played clarinet better than me and influenced me a little bit. But he called me up one day, I’m like, you know, public school. You know, I don’t want to go into it. He said — my parents weren’t on the phone it was just me. And he says, “You know you’re not supposed to play more than an hour.” And it put the fear into me. So I had years of being afraid of playing. Even now I mean I have a house, but the lady downstairs is very sweet. She says, “Play all you want you sound great.” And she’s like two floors away from me. It’s just me and my wife. So I have total freedom now. But for years in other places you’d have to wait until they’d go out of the house for groceries, and after playing with Blood, Sweat & Tears and all this stuff — so I own my own house too so it wasn’t a problem, but a lot of times there’s been that kind of anxiety, that fear of not — being sensitive to other people, not having them bother me.

It reminds me there’s an anecdote about Bix Beiderbecke when he was living, near the end of his life, and he was playing in this house where he was staying and he thought he was bothering people and they go, “No, no, keep playing.”
We’re sensitive.
They like you.

On Coltrane I heard he used to play at hotels, and I tell a couple of students, just fingering for an hour before 9:00 or whatever. So I say this is a real test because you can’t cheat yourself. If you play a C sharp major scale, or any scale [scats] really fast, you can just think of “Jada” and play it on your horn and some notes come out quicker than the others, so it really focuses you. It’s a great thing. I only did it once or twice. The other thing I wanted to say about growing up, the influence, besides naturally loving music in my heart, not knowing, it was just there, when I was about seven I saw Satchmo, Louis Armstrong, playing with his group on TV, in black & white TV when TV was new.
You had about two channels, right?

If that. I mean it was five-four-three-two — the channel comes on. But I heard them playing and I don’t remember the feeling I just remember seeing it and I said, “Mom, I want to do that.” I didn’t even know it was jazz. And I’ve told people that don’t know anything about jazz you know, if I’m playing at a concert — well I don’t want to be a teacher too much — but if I mention that I thought everybody was improvising and at a certain point they are but traditional jazz is you play a melody first, and there’s a chord progression, a sequence of chords that follow a progression. And it might be 32 bars or whatever, which is a traditional A-A-B-A form. Eight bars, eight bars, eight bars, eight bars, the bridge being bridging material, or different material. And then you want to hear the last section again, like the A section, like “Over the Rainbow.” [scats] You want to hear it again because it’s so beautiful. The bridge is different. So I tell people when Louis © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Armstrong and traditional jazz players like Charlie Parker, myself, and all those players, not the out players, they would follow the form of the tune. So they play the melody first or stay close to the melody, and then they would improvise. Whoever was improvising first, the trombone or the piano, and they’d play one chorus which is the whole tune, the form of the tune, 32 bars. And someone would say, “Okay trumpet, two choruses.” So you’d play twice through the whole form. It might take two minutes or whatever. But you play chord by chord the original sequence of the tune’s form. The other thing is with the 32 bars, I do this a lot, I re-harmonize. I change the chords. A lot of jazz composers or arrangers do that because they want to be creative. I love “Over the Rainbow” the way it is, one of the greatest tunes. But I have my own re-harm for it that I’ve never heard anybody do. It’s not about being different it’s about doing what you feel works and opens your heart.
When you’re playing on a tune like “All the Things You Are” —
I play it a lot.
Are you actually thinking, okay, I’m on G minor 7 to C 7. Are you thinking that or are you not thinking that?

That’s a very good question and I’ve mentioned this a few times to some students, and usually they don’t ask me but I’ll tell them — first of all when I was younger, and I’m a pretty good improviser, better than most at 16, there was a certain point where I started to become good, listening, transcribing. I have a whole loose leaf book of solos so I developed my ear which was so-so I think, listening to Charlie Parker, Coltrane. Even one bar, write it down. You know, Cannonball, you know, Sonny Stitt — Bird, Sonny Stitt around the same age, and Cannonball, next generation. On alto, Coltrane and Sonny Rollins. Those were my favorite. Not to negate Coleman Hawkins or Ben Webster and all those other people that are great. They didn’t have the excitement of the sixteenth notes and the more modern sound. So I went to those five people I just mentioned. Now when I listen back to old timers they sound beautiful. They’re all great. Desmond I didn’t listen to too much. He was totally innate. It was too light a sound for me. It wasn’t as exciting. Because you know, it’s just me. But as far as that goes, when I was younger, “All the Things You Are” I couldn’t play that tune too well on alto. I was playing piano too. For some reason the chord progression confused my mind. The first eight bars repeat in a different key and then the bridge is different and then it goes back to the first eight with a tag of four bars. When I play that tune now I’m being cocky when I say this, but I own that tune. There are certain tunes that I’ve played so much that, and I tell the students, I’m not thinking chord by chord anymore, on piano, even saxophone. I kind of see the chords. I know chords very well. But I’m hearing the whole line for four or eight bars when I play and I’m not playing the same thing all the time. But I just hear that. It’s like you © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

know the scene is coming up. Like if you’re in a boat and you’re going out to a destination, you know what you are seeing. You can see it, or imagine getting off the boat and walking in the sand and you reach the hotel or something. Whatever. I can kind of see that.
You can play or think a few measures ahead?

[Scats] You know I just keep going. And it’s not about playing a lot of notes but I can do that and I show students, “Look, a good lick, Miles Davis played [scats]” — it sounds hip but it’s just as good as playing twenty notes. The other weird thing for me, and again I’m not bragging about it I just told a few people, if they even understand, something happened to me. You get older and things change, just life experience, I can’t even explain it. But maybe in the last ten years, I can’t even measure that. I can play long on piano and saxophone, long sixteenth note phrases. Whereas before I copied Sonny Stitt or whoever, and I had his licks plus a couple of mine, maybe I dovetailed them together but there was a stopping point, like a wall that came up [scats]. But now I can play two or three times longer. It’s like there’s no barrier. It’s like the wall got broken in the iron curtain or something. It’s crazy. And it’s not a bragging thing, I just — it’s like string players can play forever. It’s not a breath thing unless I ran out of breath. I can just play longer now and there’s more freedom. I said wow, that’s crazy. And I don’t do it on purpose but it’s just like, no barrier.
Do you think that’s more up in your head than it is figures?

I just — a gift from God. I don’t know what else to say. And I never have to use it because I tell people, when I listen to Art Tatum, the only album I ever owned by him was “Piano Begins Here.” And I say it should be called “Piano Begins Here and Ends Here.” You know. I’m joking. But I don’t think there’s ever been a piano player like him. I mean Oscar Peterson is close. But for me, sometimes now he plays too many notes, both of them. I can’t do it, I’m just saying, my point with the students is if you heard me and were knocked out by my piano playing, or Herbie Hancock or anybody, and they kept playing sixteenth notes all the time, to me it’d get boring. You need variety. So [scats] or patterns [scats]. There’s any and everything goes. I mean go back to the classical composers. And I say this. Look as much as I love Charlie Parker, I’m not, what’s the word, a jazz historian. I can’t talk about the history too much, only the people I loved and some stories I heard but I can’t talk about their life and I don’t plan to. But Charlie Parker to me may be the greatest improviser of his day and he influenced everybody on all instruments, not to negate Art Tatum, but he to me was a master compiler. It was very interesting, I thought about this, because he took all the tunes of the day and all the classical he heard, and whatever other kind of music he heard, and he was a genius, incredible ear. I’m sure he had perfect pitch, but whatever. And he was able to © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
